claimBlocks.suggestedSection: A dictionary with identifiable regional voices
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Language introduction; project history; regional key; word-stem guide
claimBlocks.text: The Ojibwe People’s Dictionary centers Central Southwestern Ojibwe from Minnesota, Wisconsin and Canadian border-lakes communities. It uses a double-vowel writing system and identifies speakers and regional usage. Its word-building guide explains why an entry represents related inflected forms, rather than just one fixed spoken word. The project’s history describes collaboration with Elders and cultural collections. These features support learning while preserving differences; they do not establish a uniform standard for all Anishinaabe languages.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: A speaker’s account of documenting meaning
claimBlocks.text: Writing from her Wiikwemkoong experience, Mary Ann Naokwegijig-Corbiere describes speaker workshops that checked and expanded vocabulary for an Odawa and Eastern Ojibwe dictionary. She explains that English glosses can hide grammatical information and social context, so entry forms, examples and usage variation need careful decisions. Her account makes documentation visible as ongoing judgment and collaboration. It is an educator’s situated analysis of her project, not evidence of uniform usage across every community.

inspections.actualMaterial: Fresh direct opening/read of the actual informational and methodology pages listed in the source card. Read textual descriptions of contributor attribution and selected English biographies; no audio played.
scopeDetails: About the Ojibwe Language: full substantive naming/scope and double-vowel sections read, including regional/speaker-attribution explanation. The page explicitly states CentralSouthwestern focus in Minnesota,Wisconsin and Canadian border-lakes communities.

About the project: actual body and project goals read. Names the collaboration among speakers, university faculty/students/libraries and MinnesotaHistoricalSociety; explains development from Nichols/Nyholm print work and digital Elder recordings.

Ojibwe Voices: selected English accounts for EugeneStillday,GerriHoward andLeonaWakonabo plus GordonJourdain’s community/region metadata read. The page records Stillday’s2020death andWakonabo’s2021death, so retained present-tense wording is not accepted as current employment/activity.

Key to Regions: actual full key and explanation read. Codes identify origins of recordings and community-specific word forms; they are usage guides, not political boundaries or a census of all speakers.

Word-stem guide: actual explanatory body and displayed word-family-label table read. Explains choice of short headword forms/basic forms, word parts and related stems; no exact paradigm or full dictionary-entry collection copied.

Audio/example-sentence methodology: entire short actual body read as text. Speaker initials identify recordings; created examples may be reused for additional words; translations are often free rather than word-for-word. This is a methods reading, not a listening or pronunciation assessment.

inspections.actualMaterial: Actual primary-publisher19-page article PDF inspected in web-extracted text beyond abstract; official landing page inspected separately for author, issue and online publication date.
scopeDetails: Printed105 introduction explains the paper’s purposes;106–107 identify the author’s own Wiikwemkoong speech, family language context and teaching-related motivation for collecting undocumented words.
Printed108–109 describe repeated checking workshops and growth of the corpus; manuscript examples mark speaker attribution and identify limits in which communities’ usage could be checked.

Printed118–120 discuss the descriptive work carried by verb parts and the limits of English glosses. Examples of physical actions show why English word-by-word substitution can be ungrammatical; no exact language forms or sentences are reproduced in the proposed body.

Printed121 explicitly allows that another community may use an interjection differently from the author’s Wiikwemkoong expectations. Conclusion on121–122 calls for additional forms of learning material beyond dictionaries; author biography corroborates mother-tongue/teaching context.
Publisher landing page lists the author asMaryAnnCorbiere; end biography givesMaryAnnNaokwegijig-Corbiere. The packet preserves both rather than treating them as different contributors.
limits: This is an Indigenous-authored scholar/educator’s methods account, not a representative survey of all Odawa/Ojibwe communities or a current population/speaker count.
Project-status details and examples include2021searches and an account adapted from a2021workshop. The2026online release does not make every described database state current.

The suggested PDF citation’s104–123range and actual file ending at122 differ; no whole-page123 inspection is claimed. Internal PDF metadata title contains ForAuthorApproval, while the official journal publishes this very download; no claim of a separate reviewed edition is made.
The author biography’s doctorate year is not adopted: it differs from other context and is irrelevant to the claims here.
Published explanatory/narrative examples were read for method only; no family biography detail, restricted knowledge, story, direct quote or cultural teaching is reproduced.
The dictionary discussed is the separate NishnaabemwinOdawa/EasternOjibwe project, not the OjibwePeople’sDictionary and not a second edition of it.
inspections.countDecision: One distinct substantive authored publication about documentation; not a second count for the uninspected full Nishnaabemwin dictionary.

The Ontario constitution’s inclusive institutional definition of Anishinaabemowin, OPD’s CentralSouthwestern focus and Corbiere’s Wiikwemkoong/Odawa–EasternOjibwe project have different scopes.
Neither language-publication collaboration is itself a government or an exhaustive representation of all communities sharing Anishinaabe identity.

Where an existing Ontario paragraph compares institutional language usage with OPD, avoid duplicating the full OPD explanation across multiple sections; recalculate all cited prose and visible scopes together.
